utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. We have a delayed start today because the courtroom was occupied this morning for a longer time than anticipated. And I welcome especially Ms. Hasan to the courtroom and to this trial. It's the first time that you're here. Welcome and we hope you will enjoy it and we will have good cooperation, especially between the parties. The next witness should be brought in, if there is nothing to discuss elsewhere. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Dr. Lawrence, and to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, could you please state and spell your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Christopher Hamilton Lawrence, that is L-a-w-r-e-n-c-e.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I am a forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall testifying in the Popovic case in February of 2007?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And have you recently had the opportunity to review your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And is the transcript of your testimony true and correct, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And the transcript of your Popovic testimony, does it fairly and accurately reflect the answers you would give today if you were asked those very same questions?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Pretty much. I'd probably give a slightly different answer but they substantially are as I would give them today.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And at this stage I would ask that the testimony of this witness from the Popovic trial be admitted into evidence, and that's Exhibit P920.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The exhibit will be received with this number.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I would also at this stage offer into evidence the exhibits that were admitted through this witness in the Popovic trial, and that would be Exhibits P921 through to P932.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received with these numbers. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And Mr. President, with your leave, I would just like to read a brief summary of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Dr. Christopher Lawrence is a certified forensic pathologist from Australia. At the time he testified in the Popovic case, Dr. Lawrence was the state forensic pathologist for Tasmania, responsible for conducting autopsies for the coroner. From May through October of 1998, Dr. Lawrence was the chief forensic pathologist for the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY. He was the predecessor of OTP chief forensic pathologist Dr. John Clark who recently testified in this case. As the chief forensic pathologist, Dr. Lawrence led a team who conducted autopsies on the human remains exhumed from the mass graves associated with the fall of Srebrenica enclave and other OTP cases. The human remains that he and his team examined were recovered from the dam site near Petkovci and from seven secondary graves found along Cancari Road, Hodzici Road, near Zeleni Jadar and in Liplje. The autopsies were performed at a morgue in Visoko, in Bosnia. The human remains exhumed from these mass graves were delivered in body bags to the morgue for Dr. Lawrence and his team to examine. Some of the body bags contained complete bodies, and other body bags contained body parts. After photographing the contents of the body bags, the pathologists examined the human remains for bullets, fractures and boney abnormalities using a fluoroscope, which is a device that produces an x-ray image. After searching the bodies for personal items and removing the clothing which was handed over to the crime scene officers for further examination, Dr. Lawrence and his team examined the bodies and bones and photographed any evidence of injury. Any damaged bones were handed over to the anthropologists for reconstruction. Upon receiving these reconstructed bones, the pathologists examined them for injury, and in the case of an apparent gun-shot injury, attempted to trace the track of the bullet. In most instances, the pathologist examined the clothing to determine whether the damage to the clothing corroborated the injuries identified. Dr. Lawrence prepared a report for each grave site containing his findings and his opinion as to the cause of death of the victims. The cause of death for the majority of the victims whose bodies were complete were gun-shot wounds. Some of the victims sustained shot-gun wounds and wounds caused by shrapnel. Most of the shrapnel wounds were sustained by victims who had been recovered from the Zeleni Jadar secondary grave site. In conducting the autopsies, Dr. Lawrence and his team retrieved ligatures and blindfolds from the human remains. The majority of the ligatures were tied around the wrists and arms of the victims. In some cases, the arms were clearly secured behind the body. Some of the blindfolds that were recovered were found loose inside the body bags, others were still positioned around the heads and covering the eyes of the victims. That concludes my summary, and if I may, I'll proceed with my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, before I start with my questions, I notice that you have some documents with you. Could you please tell us what those are?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: These are my copies of the reports that I prepared from the -- for the separate grave sites and a summary of those reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And you're entitled to refer to your notes, but just for the benefit of everyone in the courtroom, if you can tell us if you're referring to them and what it is that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, when did you obtain your certification as a forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I qualified as a forensic pathologist in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And could you please tell us what your current occupation is?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I am the state forensic pathologist for Tasmania.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And since when have you held that post?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Since February 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And could you just briefly describe your responsibilities as a state forensic pathologist for Tasmania?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: My responsibilities are to perform medical examinations on sudden, unexpected, unnatural, and violent deaths for the coroner and to describe the circumstances of the death.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we go now back to 1998, what were your principal duties as chief pathologist for the OTP from May through October of 1998?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: My chief responsibilities as chief pathologist were to examine the remains that had been exhumed, to establish the cause of death, and to establish details regarding the circumstances of the death.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the state of the human remains were that you were tasked with examining?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: The remains were quite extensively decomposed. The bodies had been dead for three years. They varied to some degree in how decomposed. In some of the bodies, there were still quite a large amount of soft tissue remaining. In others, the bodies were completely skeletalised. In addition, the bodies -- some of the bodies were fairly complete, that is, they had a head, chest, abdomen, limbs, and some were quite disrupted, where the relationship between the body parts had been disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If you could just clarify what you mean by disrupted?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: When a body decomposes, the tissues, the ligaments and the material that hold the limbs and arms and head together break down and the body parts can become dis-attached. Consequently, in some of the grave sites and particularly sites such as the dam site and Liplje, the bodies were quite badly disarticulated, that is, the joints had been separated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And did you examine all of these various forms of human remains that you received?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes, we examined all of the largely whole bodies and all of the large body parts. In the first half of the year, in the dam site, in Cancari Road 12 and 3, every single body bag was examined by a pathologist. In the case of Hodzici Road 3, 4 and 5, Liplje and Zeleni Jadar, some of the very small body parts were examined by anthropologists and only examined by the pathologists if there was significant damage or if there were significant body parts. The reason for this change was to deal with the large volume of material that we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in regards to the body parts that you received, did you attempt to match any much the parts before conducting your autopsies?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: When considering the body parts, I had information from Professor Wright as to the location of where the body parts were recovered, and we attempted, as best we could, to try and associate the body parts, but the reality was that it was actually quite difficult to associate them. So consequently, we ended up with a lot of body parts which were quite difficult to reassociate. The only real practical way that could have been done was with DNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And was DNA analysis or technology available to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Some DNA material was taken in cases where there were documents which indicated a provisional identification. But there was fairly limited DNA taken. At that stage there was not a lab in the country which was capable of performing that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: As regards those body parts that you were not able to reconcile or match, did you attempt to render an opinion as to the cause of death of the individual from whom that body part came from?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: We examined the body parts to see if they had gun-shot injuries that would be capable of causing the death of the individual from which that body part came. Now, of course, the problem was we had far more body parts than we had bodies, and so therefore, to some degree, trying to give a cause of death on a body part was somewhat illogical. I have attempted in my reports to give causes of death on the largely intact bodies because that's more meaningful. However, we did examine the body parts because we wanted to establish whether or not gun-shot wounds were present.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Were there instances where you were able to tell from examining a body part that you were able to determine the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes. There were some cases, for example, an isolated head, where there was a gun-shot wound going through the head, would clearly be a cause of death in that particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, what killed most of the victims that you examined?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: If we look at the -- sorry, I'm just referring to my notes here, the 254 essentially intact bodies, of them, 203 showed a cause of death of gun-shot wounds. One of them showed gun-shot and shrapnel wounds. And in 50 of those cases, the cause of death was undetermined.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: How were you able to identify a gun-shot wound or what criteria did you use?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: We used a number of criteria. The first was the finding of a bullet embedded in the tissue or bone on X-ray. The second was examining -- was finding bullet tracks, that is, the path of the bullet passing through soft tissue. This is in the case of bullets -- where the bullet has probably exited the body. And the third group in which we concluded there was a gun-shot wound were cases where there were fragments of metal from the bullet and fracturing of the bones in that area. Those were the criteria we used to identify gun-shot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in reviewing your reports I noticed that you refer to probable and possible gun-shot wounds. Can you tell us what you classified as a probable or possible gun-shot wound?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: The cases that we listed as gun-shot wounds were ones where we were very confident that the information we had indicated a gun-shot wound. In some cases, we were able to find small fragments of metal, which looked like a gun-shot wound but may not have been. And in those cases we called them possible gun-shot wounds. In other cases, we found a defect, for example, in the skull, which would correspond to the damage one would expect to find from a gun-shot wound but could not find a projectile, and in those cases we would call that a probable gun-shot wound.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And why, in your view, did you think it significant to report those findings?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I think we were trying to give the Court as much information as we could. These are -- these were difficult bodies to examine. They were quite badly decomposed and because they had been buried, dug up and reburied, they were quite significantly separated. I wanted to convey particularly in those cases like the dam site or Liplje, where the bodies were quite badly separated, that even despite the fact that we had very few whole bodies, there were significant numbers of gun-shot wounds in those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm just going to move now to a slightly different topic and ask you whether any of the human bones that you received, were any of them damaged or fractured?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes. A large number of the bones were damaged and fractured. Some of them by the gun-shot wounds, and some of them by damage which had occurred after death, either during the first burial, the -- the exhumation, the second burial or the re-exhumation again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And how was it that you were able to identify injuries in those fractured or damaged bones?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Well, there are a number of injuries that we were looking for. The first kind of injury we were looking for were injuries that occurred at the time of death. And in those cases we were looking for things like gun-shot wounds and we were looking for the presence or absence of haemorrhage. Now again because the bodies were so badly decomposed, it was quite difficult to identify haemorrhage. However, in a small number of cases we were able to demonstrate that there was haemorrhage present and that these injuries had occurred at the time of death. There is a diagram -- there is a picture of one of these that might be a good illustration of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us where that picture is?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: This would be in the report for Cancari Road 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P924.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have that on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you just give us the page number?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Sorry, the page number is -- sorry, it is after page 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if you wouldn't mind, there is a -- I don't think it's in your copy. Do you have a stamp number on there? No.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: No, I don't, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was that page 18, Dr. Lawrence?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: It was -- it's the photograph following page 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It's page 41 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in this photograph, Dr. Lawrence -- sorry, it's not up on the screen yet. Okay. I think we have it on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What is it that we see here?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: What you can see is the top of the head, the skull has been opened, you can see under the skull the brain. Surrounding the brain there is a large amount of haemorrhage and the arrow demonstrates a bullet. Now, again, trying to ascertain whether an injury has occurred at the time of death relies on the presence of haemorrhage. Most of these bodies were too decomposed to see haemorrhage, but in some of the better preserved bodies, and this is an example of it, you could actually see haemorrhage. This is clearly an injury that has occurred at the time of death, and is almost -- is undoubtedly the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the skull that we see here looks like it's a fairly intact skull, apart from the portion of it that has been removed.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Removed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in those cases where you received completely fractured bones, how did you go about identifying injuries in those?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: In the bones that were badly broken, the anthropologists would reconstruct the skull using superglue to demonstrate the defects.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And may we have Exhibit P924, e-court page 18, displayed on the screen. And that would be page 18 on the B/C/S version as well. Perhaps we can rotate that 90 degrees to the right, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This is a photograph that is in your report relating to Cancari Road site 12?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what's depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: This shows the back of the skull. You can see that there are lots of fractures in it, and there is white material which is the glue that we used to reconstruct the skull. What you can see there demonstrated by the pointer and the arrow is a gun-shot wound of entrance and a gun-shot wound of exit on the other side of the skull. This would not have been obvious in the skull as we had received it, but after reconstruction the holes became obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And who was responsible for reconstructing?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: The reconstructions were carried out by the anthropologists.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. So in a case like this, were you able to determine the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes. I would be confident that the cause of death would be a gun-shot wound, a wound like this would be rapidly fatal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now you mentioned earlier that you were not able to determine the cause of death in some instances. Can you explain to us why that wasn't possible?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: In some of the bodies, we could not identify sufficient injury to account for death. I suspect that the reason that we were unable to do so is because we were missing gun-shot wounds that were present. In wounds that passed, say, for example, through the abdomen and did not strike bone, in a skeletalised remain it's impossible to tell whether or not the person had been shot. We did carry out examinations of the clothing and from looking at the clothing we could identify a lot more bullet holes in the clothing than we could identify in the bodies. However, I would never use the clothing to determine a cause of death because one cannot be certain where it was in relation to the body when the damage was caused. So in -- I guess in summary, I think it is highly likely that most of the cases where we couldn't determine a cause of death, it is most likely that they died from gun-shot wounds that we just couldn't detect.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And -- okay. We have been discussing a lot now about cause of death. I'm just going to move to another concept. Are you familiar with the phrase "manner of death"?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And could you please define that for us, your understanding of it?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: In forensic pathology work, one normally talks about the cause of death as being the disease, process or injury which actually produced death. And then we talk about a concept of the manner of death. Now, this is a partly legal concept but we are talking about whether the death was natural, accidental, suicidal, homicidal. It's really the circumstances -- it relates to the circumstances surrounding the death.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And is there a relationship between cause of death and manner of death, and if there is one, can you tell us -- can you explain that interrelationship?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: The answer -- one -- in almost inevitably considers the manner of death in considering the cause of death. But in the coronial system in which Dr. Clark and myself work. It would normally be the role of the pathologist to establish the cause of death and it would normally be the role of the coroner, who is a magistrate, to establish the manner of death. The pathologist might be expected to advise the coroner on the manner of death, as when you're considering the circumstances of the death, you do have to consider the manner, but it is not, strictly speaking, the role of the pathologist to establish that. Now, I -- in other jurisdictions, and I spent two years working in the United States, the forensic pathologists in the United States, in the medical examiner systems usually have to establish both the cause and the manner of death. So, for example, in a case of a gun-shot wound, one would normally give a cause of death as being gun-shot wounds and the manner as being homicide.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And based on your experience, is it possible to determine the manner of death when the cause of death is unknown?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: In some cases, yes, but often no. If I can give an example, one might have a, as I had in the United States, case where a person had been buried in a clandestine grave and was quite badly decomposed. It was not clear exactly what had caused death. But I concluded because of the nature of the way the body had been concealed that the manner of death was homicide. So it is possible to have an undetermined cause of death and a determined manner of death but it's not particularly common.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Aside from cause of death, is there anything else that you found in your examinations that would assist in determining the manner of death?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I think there was a fair amount of circumstantial material in these examinations. This relates to the presence of ligatures or wrist bindings, the presence of blindfolds, material such as, in some particular cases, and I'm thinking in particular in Cancari Road 12 we had three cases where there appeared to be deliberate targeting of the joints of the body in what appeared to be an attempt to cause pain, where there were deliberate shooting of the shoulders, the elbows, the wrists, the knees, in a pattern which did not -- which looked deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if -- you've just mentioned ligatures and blindfolds --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd just like to turn to Exhibit P928 and page 16 of that exhibit in the English version, and it's also page 16 in the B/C/S version. If it's also possible to just rotate that one to the right, 90 degrees to the right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, can you just tell us what we see here depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes. This is a body. It is the -- the person is lying face down, at the bottom you can see, above the writing, you can see the belt. What you can see there are the arms, which are behind the back. You can see the watch band which shows the left wrist. And just above that, there is a cord ligature which is tying the wrists together. This is an example of one of the bodies where the hands had been tied behind the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we could turn to Exhibit P927, and that's another photograph. It's at page 18 in the English version, and page 20 of the B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, can you also tell us in this photograph what we are seeing here?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes. What you can see here is the top of the skull. It has been reconstructed. What you can see there is the blindfold which is running around the head, the eyes are at the front, and in the blindfold you can see a defect. In the underlying skull, there is a gun-shot wound. This is an indication that the blindfold was in this particular site when the gun-shot was inflicted, indicating that it is, in fact, a blindfold.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us that these blindfolds and ligatures are some of the items that tell you about the circumstances of the deaths. Aside from what you've taken, what you've surmised from these items, did you obtain any other information about the circumstances surrounding the deaths of the victims from any other sources?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I'm not specifically sure to what you're referring.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. My question comes from having read your reports. You make reference therein to having received some information from OTP investigators.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was given the alleged circumstances of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And to what extent did you take that information that you received into account during the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Whenever I'm doing my work, I try and get as much information about the circumstances before I start my examination. And then I carry out my examination. Now, obviously, information that you are provided may be wrong, and it is my normal practice to try and test whether or not the story I have been told is correct or incorrect by looking at the physical evidence. That is, one takes the information that you're provided with, which may or may not be correct, and you test it against what you've seen. The aim being to try and prove or disprove whether the story is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Lawrence. Those would be all my questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And Mr. President, that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Hasan. Mr. Tolimir, your cross-examination, please. Before you commence your cross-examination, Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted some clarification on one point that you've made in your evidence. At page 13, line 4 to 7, you are quoted as saying: "I guess in summary, I think it is highly likely that most of the cases where we couldn't determine the cause of death, it is most likely that they died from gun-shot wounds that we just couldn't detect."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Is that a conclusion? You make a conclusion in -- you're saying in this that you made the conclusion that the cause of death was nevertheless gun-shot wounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In my practice in Australia, I would draw a distinction between something that I was certain about and something that I thought was highly probable. In this particular instance, I have given you the causes of death in those cases which I am certain about, and the others are either possible or probable but I'm not certain about them. I have therefore given you both pieces of information. I am just explaining that I think it's likely that those other ones are gun-shot wounds, but I don't think I can prove it to the standard of proof that I would normally be required in a court of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence would like to wish peace in this house to all those present and to Mr. Lawrence, and would like to have this Court proceedings completed not as I wish but as God wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation} Mr. Lawrence, I'm going to be putting questions to you about certain things in your report that were perhaps not quite clear. So I hope you will bear with me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P923 in the e-court now, please? This is an expert report about the remain -- the autopsy of human remains from the Brana locality. I'm interested in page 2, paragraph 4, of this report. The date of the report is June 1998. Thank you. Page 2, paragraph 4. Thank you. We don't see it yet. Can we rotate it? Thank you. Page 2, please, paragraph 4. While we are waiting for the page to be shown -- thank you. Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for this, you will probably be able to answer because you have your copy of the report in front of you as well. Based on anthropological assessment -- this is what it states in paragraph 4, based on the anthropological assessment, it can be concluded that one person was between 13 and 18 years of age; three were between the age of 18 and 25; and 42 were older than 25. My question is: Did you personally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should clarify if we have the right page in B/C/S on the screen. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have it and it's on the first page. In the English, it's the correct page. In the B/C/S -- in the Serbian, it's not correct. That's why I read it in Serbian. Thank you. It's on the first page in English, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page is it in B/C/S, Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that in the Serbian, on the right-hand side, it seems that we have the wrong report. Since now we are talking about the report on the exhumations and autopsies of human remains from the dam site. And on the right side, in the Serbian, the report we are looking at is the one from the Hodzici locality. I think that's what the mistake is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, while the technical service processes this -- well, all right, now it's okay. Thank you very much. I apologise to you, sir. You can answer: Were you, yourself, the one who made these estimates or assessments of the age, and what were the techniques that you used to establish the time of -- the age of the persons at the time of death as they are reported here in your findings? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: No. These were not my personal findings. They are information that was provided by Mr. Baraybar, and the estimates were based on the estimation of age using the epiphyses of the bones, the symphysis pubis, and the fourth ribs. I included them in my report purely to provide background information regarding the age of some of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We had the opportunity recently to have Mr. Baraybar here and he explained in detail what you just mentioned, the technique used to establish the age of the victims. I would like to ask you now to look at paragraph 7 now in the English, and also paragraph 7 in the Serbian version. And where you say that there were no complete bodies at the Brana -- the dam locality. And now we go to paragraph 7, where it says: "There were parts of 46 individuals in the grave. Because of the separation of the body parts, these were collected in 91 body bags. This is in the report by Professor Wright. None of the bodies were complete. And it obviously cannot be guaranteed that the body bags are from separate individuals. Because the individual bodies could not be reconstructed, I have given a cause of death for the body parts in each body bag rather than each individual. It is possible that a divided individual, for example, separate head and torso, might be given more than one cause of death." In view of what is written here, and earlier we've seen that the number of persons was established and the cause of death, but when we are talking about the cause of death, the cause of death was determined for body parts and not for individuals, can you please explain what the number of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is asked to repeat the rest of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, at the moment we are not receiving interpretation. The last sentence was not heard by the interpreters. The transcript stopped with the sentence: "... the cause of death was determined for body parts and not for individuals. Can you please explain what the number of --" and there it stops. Can you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How did you come -- I repeat, how did you then come to the data about the total number of individuals and the cause of death? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I think the dam site represents one of the more difficult sites that we dealt with. The bones were extremely badly damaged. They were very badly disarticulated and the bodies were very decomposed. I think I've indicated in this information that in this particular site, even though we had approximately 46 individuals, we could only really give a cause of death in four of them as gun-shot wounds, and that 81 of the body bags had an undetermined cause of death. This is largely because the bodies were so badly broken up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show paragraph 5 on page 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In this paragraph, the following is stated: "Ligatures of rope were found on the -- in the grave site." My question is: What is the reason that the items were not investigated in the morgue but that they were returned to The Hague? And can you please tell us whether these items were returned and was there an expert report written on them? And I read from paragraph 6: "There was twine ligatures found in the grave similar to others found at LPO 2 and CRO 3 sites and a possible blindfold. These were sent to The Hague and were not examined at the morgue." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just back up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last part was a quotation from number 6 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, you mean paragraph number 6, not paragraph number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was, I think, a misrepresentation at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Yes, a number of the ligatures found in the grave not definitely associated with the bodies were sent back to The Hague and not sent to the mortuary. I examined these later on, when I returned to The Hague, to ascertain whether or not they were similar to the ligatures that we examined in Liplje and also some in CR 3, Cancari Road 3. It was my opinion, looking at them, that they were similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to say on what basis you came to that conclusion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: The appearances of the twine used, the appearances of the knots used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You did not precisely answer why the items were sent to The Hague before being processed in the morgue. Should not the expert examination have been carried out on the items in the morgue first before they were sent to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: That would have been my preference. This was a decision made by the people at the scene, to send them to The Hague not to the mortuary, but that's why I carried out the later examination at The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you help us and tell us who made this decision? Was it your decision to send them to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not my decision. I'm not sure who made that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Precisely, Witness. When you say that the bodies are brought to The Hague, what does this actually mean? Does this mean that these are brought to the OTP or to the mortuary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, we are not talking here about bodies but about the ligatures that were found in the grave. The ligatures were transported back to The Hague. It would have been my preference for those ligatures to have been transported to the mortuary but that did not occur. At the time the examination -- the -- at the time the exhumation was occurring at the dam, I was still at The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I misread the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you to Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, was this is a decision made by experts, by pathologists, anthropologists, for the ligatures to be taken to The Hague, because you said that you felt it would have been better to have examined them there? Or was that somebody else who made that decision? I assume that you are unable to tell the Judges exactly who that was.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: As I say, at this stage, I was still at The Hague and not in Bosnia. I am not sure who made that decision, but I did indicate at that stage to those managing the exhumation site that I would prefer to see that sort of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us who was heading the exhumation work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: The exhumation team was headed by Professor Richard Wright at the time. However, I'm not sure whether the decision was made by him or by the investigators in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Richard Wright have experts who could have carried out this task at the morgue down there in the graves, where the other examinations were carried out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Professor Wright worked at the exhumation site. He did not work at the mortuary. From memory, I believe that he did have some scene of crimes officers at the site who could have carried out some examination of these ligatures. But since I was not there at the time, I can't tell you much more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise to the interpreters. Are you able to tell us if at any point you saw the expert findings that the expert people in The Hague were supposed to look at regarding those ligatures that had been sent by the people who were working under the leadership of Mr. Wright?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: What expert findings?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they examined -- why were they sent to The Hague? What was the purpose of that? Are you able to tell us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I don't know why they were sent to The Hague. I did examine them later at The Hague, but I would have preferred to examine them in the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, are you able to tell us who other than Professor Wright was authorised to send material directly to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I was not in charge of the exhumation site. You'd have to ask somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lawrence. I understand you. I was just asking about the position that could have made the decision in this case, but I understand your answer when you say that you would have preferred to have examined them on the scene. And can we now see -- each one of your reports describes the autopsy procedure. This is on page 5 in the Serbian, and page 4 in the English. So each of your reports describes the autopsy procedure or the protocol. Were there differences in the autopsy procedures that were applied during the examination of body parts from different grave sites, or were the same procedures applied in all of the cases? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: As a general rule, the procedures were the same. However, in the dam site, in Cancari 12, Cancari 3, all of the body bags were examined by a pathologist. After these case -- after these sites, when we started dealing with Hodzici Road, Liplje and Zeleni Jadar, we were dealing with many more body bags, we had much larger teams working, and we were starting to have concerns that we may not be able to finish the procedure in time. As a consequence of this, a decision was made at the suggestion of Mr. Baraybar, that some of the smaller body parts be examined primarily by an anthropologist rather than the pathologist. It was generally felt that the whole bodies gave us the most useful information, and that the pathologists should spend their time dealing with the whole bodies and the large body parts, while the small body parts could initially be examined by the anthropologist. Where the anthropologist felt that there was a significant injury or where, for example, that part was a head, the remains would be -- then also be examined by a pathologist to ascertain whether there -- what injuries were present. But essentially so it meant that the Hodzici Road, Liplje and Zeleni Jadar cases, some of the smaller body bags were not actually examined by a pathologist unless the anthropologist found a significant injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now look at item 11. And in my copy it states: "The clothing was listed, labelled with a metal tag with the case number, and placed in a container prior to washing." My question is: Mr. Lawrence, are you able to tell us if the clothing, before it was washed, was examined in any way? For example, were there -- was it examined for traces of gunpowder or similar tests? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes. The body was examined -- sorry, the body was X-rayed fully clothed and then examined fully clothed, before the clothes were taken off for washing. Unfortunately, because of the large amount of decompositional fluid and dirt, it was almost impossible to identify gun-shot residue. I think there was only one case in the 883 bodies where we -- where I saw anything that even remotely resembled gunpowder residue, but even there, we were far from certain as to whether it was gunpowder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us why the clothing wasn't subjected to any other examination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: It was -- at the time we were doing this examination, it was felt that the clothing might provide one of the few means of identification of a large number of cases. Under the circumstances, it was felt to be more useful to clean the clothes in order to allow the families to identify the clothing than it was to find gunpowder residue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did this affect the quality of your work, in view of the required procedures? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: That -- that is hard to answer that question. I do not believe so. I think it is unlikely that analysis of the clothing for gunpowder residue would have changed our conclusions regarding this. However, I accept that in a normal case of a well-preserved body, without decomposition, that that examination would occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lawrence. Could you please now look at paragraph 12?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can I have the next page in the Serbian, in the e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Paragraph 12 states: "After or once the body was undressed, it was washed and rephotographed. Where necessary, soft tissue was removed from the body or bones and a careful examination for injuries was made." My question is: Why was it necessary to remove soft tissue from the body or bones? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: In a body that is intact, where the skin is complete, one can normally tell where the gun-shot wound is without problem. Most of these bodies did not have complete skin coverage because of the decomposition. It was therefore necessary to dissect the tissue to see whether there was, in fact, a bullet track in the soft tissue because the loss of the skin made it difficult to identify the gun-shot wounds on the skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand you correctly? You established whether there were any wounds or injuries only on the basis of the bone? And that is also what you used to establish the cause of death? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: No. The wounds were established on the basis of examination of the skin, the soft tissue, the bone and the X-ray examination of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could an x-ray, then, help to establish the trajectory of the bullet through the skin, the soft tissue, the flesh? Why was it necessary to do this? I didn't understand it well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Again, in a body that was fully -- was in a normal state, it would be my practice to first of all X-ray to establish the passage of the bullet; secondly, examine the skin to examine the entrance and exit wounds; and then to carry out an internal examination to establish that the entrance and exit wounds were connected in the way that they appeared to be. It is my normal practice to carry out both an external and an internal examination in all gun-shot wounds. It is also necessary to carry out an internal examination to recover the projectile as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Lawrence, for this additional explanation. I wanted things cleared up completely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 12 in Serbian and page 9 in English. We need to see the passage with the subheading "peri-mortem injuries". That's injuries that occurred around the time of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your report, you divide these wounds into indisputably gun fire; second, probable gun-shot wounds; and, three, certainly not or possible gun-shot wounds. Based on what did you divide wounds into these three categories?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just trying to find where you're referring to in the English. Oh, sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't turn on the microphone. You see above the table, the numbers 1, 2 and 3? These lines contain the information I just read.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And my question was: On what basis did you determine this gradation, whether a wound was definitely gun-shot, probable gun-shot or possible gun-shot?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Again, in this particular site, we were dealing with quite severely fragmented bones. There were some wounds where I was convinced by the shape of the wound, the presence of the bevelling under the wound, and the adjacent damage, that it was certainly a gun-shot wound. There were other cases where I either had small fragments of metal on X-ray adjacent to roughly circular fractures. These I concluded -- I was uncomfortable to call them definite gun-shot wounds but given the presence of the metal fragments and the nature, I thought they were probably gun-shot wounds. And then there were some where I wasn't certain. I thought it's possible they might be. There were fractures that looked possibly consistent with there may have been some metal fragments nearby but I would be by no means certain that they are gun-shot wounds. And those I would call possible gun-shot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did you understand firearms to mean anything that could fire or just rifle rounds? Did you include mortar shells and other type of weapons?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Generally in these reports, I talked about gun-shot wounds, shot-gun wounds, and shrapnel. In the instance that I was talking about gun-shot wounds, I would not include ordnance such as mortars and artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we must have our first break now. And we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lawrence, before we left off, you used two terms, one was "gun-shot" and the other "shot-gun." Could you please explain the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I usually restrict the term "gun-shot" to rifled weapons, that is, weapons that make the bullet spin as it's fired. These would be revolvers, handguns, rifles and so forth. And shot-guns, where the barrels are unrifled and they fire small pellets of lead. Those are the two terms that I use in regard to the kinds of gun-shot wounds we are talking about. And that's what I meant by the distinction between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could I now ask e-court to display P942? Sorry, 924. It's a report on the examination of mortal remains from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear where.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the locality Cancarski Put number 12, carried out in August 1998, page 10 in Serbian and in English. We need the passage titled, "Report."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, the title of this report is related to Cancari Road, site 12.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can't see the version in English on the screen, so it's difficult for the witness to follow. Both are in Serbian. Could you show the witness the English version, please? There it is. Paragraph 2 under subheading "Reports." I will now be quoting from paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Each autopsy is entirely the responsibility of the pathologist performing the autopsy. There was discussion between pathologists and the anthropologists on each case. I was present in the autopsy room for most of the autopsies and was available at all times for discussion. The opinions expressed in the report are entirely those of the pathologist in charge of the case. This accounts for any apparent variations in expression of findings or opinion. "The anthropology team made formal reports of stature, sex and age. The data upon which these opinions were based is contained in the original notes of the appropriate anthropologist." Now, when you mention "autopsy report," does that term comprise the findings of the pathologist and the anthropologist both and are they integrated into one report?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: The autopsy report is the work of the pathologist. The anthropologists prepared a separate report. However, the anthropologists did give advice to the pathologists about their view on the injuries, and that would have been integrated into the autopsy report prepared by the pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the pathologist able to submit his findings if it contradicted a finding by the anthropologist? And what was done in case the pathologist and the anthropologist disagreed?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: The pathologist had the final decision regarding the assessment of the injuries. In the event that there was a disagreement between the anthropologist and the pathologist, they would normally consult me, and we would reach a consensus about what was said. If an agreement could not be reached, the opinion expressed was that of the pathologist who did the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lawrence. Since you said that the pathologist's findings were final and authoritative, can you tell me what could then have been the cause of such disagreement? Do you have an example? And was there one single uniform model for making reports? Or was it possible that injuries were described differently from report to report?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: That's a multiple-part question. The pathologists varied in their experience of dealing with boney injuries. And most of the pathologists would listen to the anthropologists' opinions in these cases. I can recall some discussions between myself and Mr. Baraybar in relation to some of the injuries that would be classified as possible or probable gun-shot wounds. For example, where you might have a defect that didn't have all of the normal characteristics of a gun-shot wound but might have some fragments of metal. Those are the sorts of things that might occur. There were also occasional questions about whether there was a blunt force injury, a fracturing, which was -- and whether it was, in fact, a blunt force or whether it was -- occurred as a consequence of a gun-shot wound. There was no uniform -- the models -- the report that was hand-filled out was a sort of a pro forma document that people filled in the gaps. The pathologists for the most part worked for about two weeks, and when they first came to work, I would sit down with them and go through how we interpreted the wounds, what we would call a possible, probable gun-shot wound, those sorts of things. So there was some uniformity. However, there was considerable latitude for description, and I encouraged the pathologists to write what they thought they saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up in e-court page 22 in Serbian and in English. The part under the subheading, "Shrapnel." We see it in English. It's the second paragraph from below. And the same in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say halfway down the paragraph: "The fragments looked unlike bullet core fragments and resembled fragments of shrapnel from shells or mortar rounds recovered from around Sarajevo. Field bandages," et cetera. You mention mortar and artillery shells found around Sarajevo. Why is this mentioned here? Is that a mistake in the report or is it a reference to some prior experience of yours or maybe the pathologist who did this?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: No. Most of the pathologists who were dealing with these cases would not have seen a large number of shrapnel-related injuries. Quite a number of the gun-shot -- the bullets in the gun-shot wounds were fragmented, and I considered it important to try and distinguish between fragments of bullet and fragments of ordnance, shrapnel. Because of the lack of experience in the pathologists, I obtained some examples of shrapnel from around Sarajevo to give them an example of what it might look like. What we routinely did was test the material with a magnet to establish whether it was a ferrous material or not and also compare it to these fragments obtained from Sarajevo for purposes of comparison. We did not have a ballistics expert from the police present at the time, and so I used the material from Sarajevo really as a reference sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the first part you said pathologists or at least some pathologists did not have sufficient experience. Could you explain in greater detail what you meant by that? Because perhaps I missed something or perhaps I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes. The pathologists came from England, Scotland, Ireland, France, Germany. Most of them had not seen substantial numbers of people who had been injured with shrapnel because of their practice. They would be familiar with gun-shot wounds but they would not routinely see many shrapnel injuries. The only exceptions would probably have been the pathologists from Northern Ireland who would be familiar with bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This leads us again to the problem of the distance of fire. If it's shrapnel, then it's easy to conclude that the weapon was relatively far away; but if a rifle round was fired from 500 metres away, or 50 metres away, or a thousand metres away, would the pathologists have enough experience and skill to determine the distance from which a firearm round was fired?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I think I have indicated in my report that assessment of range of fire was pretty much a lost cause in these particular cases. I really do not believe, given the state of the bodies, that we could realistically tell very much about the range of fire at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you share with us your opinion on this: Would the range of fire in these cases that you have worked on be then considered undetermined? And that concerns 183 [as interpreted] cases, as you said. Because it is important to us whether and how many people were killed in combat and others were shot without participating in combat. How could we determine the difference between the two groups?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Those are, again, a number of questions. If I can take them in order, about all a pathologist can tell about range of fire is, firstly, if the muzzle of the gun is in contact with the body; secondly, if the weapon is -- the muzzle of the gun is between a centimetre and a metre. Once it gets beyond that, the pathologist can't tell you anything about the range of fire. So I think it is correct, I would give the range of fire in all of these cases as undetermined. Now, in regard to -- I'm sorry, I'm -- sorry, I'm just trying to answer the rest of your questions. In regard to how could we tell the difference between people who were killed in combat and others who were shot without participating in combat, I have a number of propositions. The first is that if these people were people killed in combat, why was such -- why was such trouble taken to conceal these bodies and why were they transported so far from the sites where they were initially killed? If they were combatants, how do you explain the presence of the blindfolds and ligatures? If they were combatants, how do you account for young children and very old men? If they were combatants, how do you account for people who have got hip replacements, spines so badly damaged that they would be incapable of easy movement, people who have had operations to remove their larynx so that they have what is called a tracheostomy in their throat? In my opinion, these people are unlikely to be combatants. The other thing I think in general terms in modern combat is that one expects most of the fatalities to be due to shrapnel wounds and not to gun-shot wounds, and so the percentage of gun-shot wounds in these deaths is unusually high for modern combat. In addition, in Cancari Road 12, I saw a number of people who were clearly injured and who had bandages on, including one man who had shrapnel injuries in the liver and in the right-hand, who had bandages on those injuries, who then had a ligature on the wrist and had been subsequently shot. So I think it is likely that this is an injured person who had been medically treated and had then been killed. Again, I don't believe that these people were combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, may I interrupt you? In your last question, you said, "Would the range of fire in these cases that you have worked on be then considered undetermined? And that concerns 183 cases, as you said." This is page 36, lines 1 through 3. I've tried to figure out where you found this number of 183 cases. What is your reference for that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Lawrence said that he looked at 883 bodies that underwent this entire procedure, and he said that in the previous question, that in none of the cases the range -- was the range determined, and based on that I asked my question, 883 cases. But I asked for Mr. Lawrence's expert opinion, how best to proceed when bodies were collected during clearing operations. So all the bodies were collected, those who were killed in combat and those who were fired at from close range, and placed in the same grave. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, sorry for interrupting you again. You were recorded to have said 183 cases, not 883. And I wanted to clarify if you were really using the term "183." But I think that was a mistake. You were referring to 883. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Mr. President. I put that in my question that Mr. Lawrence has answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And my next question -- it should be the number 883. 883. And my next question would be: If these points made by Mr. Lawrence are theories, were these theories included in the description from the localities that he worked on and can they help us determine how many bodies in the common graves were killed in combat, from a distance of 300/400 metres, or as opposed to those who were killed at close range, such as 2 metres, because he said that smaller differences could not be really established, such as 1 centimetre, for instance, to 1 metre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan? I saw you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I was just going to seek clarification of a point but I think we've resolved that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I've indicated that the pathologists were not really in a position to assess range of fire in most of these cases, not in any meaningful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If these are the points that you've stated, I would like to put some other questions, the ones regarding the idea of the distance of the body from locality. For example, in the case of asanacija, bodies could be brought from an area nearby or from a farther removed area and placed in the same grave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand what you mean by "asanacija."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What I mean by that is after combat, and the completion of operations, bodies are collected from the front and buried in a common grave in order to prevent an outbreak of diseases and so on and so forth. That's what I mean by the word "asanacija."

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Right. Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Is it possible, then, to bury in the same grave somebody who was killed above the grave, in the immediate vicinity of the grave, or from the front, some 1.000 or 1500 metres away? That's the question. Is it possible that such bodies could be buried together? And this is a question which corresponds to your first theory.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Hypothetically, yes, of course they could include people from them. I think the issue is the movement of the bodies from the primary site to the secondary site often seemed to be quite significant distances. For example, in the bodies that were -- the bodies that came from the Kravica warehouse were then taken to Glogova and then taken to Zeleni Jadar. These -- it seems to me surprising that these bodies would be moved these sorts of distances if they were just combat fatalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lawrence. Many things are illogical to me as well. This is why I'm asking you, in order to get an explanation. I'm not asking because I'm looking for some kind of illogical matters in your statement. I'm just asking about all the things that are not clear to me. The second thing you mentioned was that -- how to explain the presence of ligatures. So I'm asking you now: Is it possible that somebody with a ligature could be brought to this primary or secondary grave and that they were killed with a ligature at a different location, if bodies are being collected from the battle front?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not quite sure I understand that question. Can you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, as your second proposition, how to explain the presence of blindfolds, for example. I'm asking you now, is it possible that somebody is killed or shot at a location that is different from the location of the primary and the secondary grave, at a distance of some 5.000 -- 500 or 1.000 metres away, and then later that they are brought to the grave where also bodies are brought from other locations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I understand that you were talking about -- well, everything is possible. Is it possible, then, to have young people, old people, and the sick and the wounded brought to the same grave and so on and so forth, if the collection of casualties from the battle front is underway? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: Yes. What I meant here was that I thought it was unlikely that these young people and old people and sick people were -- and the wounded people were combatants. Hence, the question comes up: How did they get killed? It would not -- if they weren't combatants, they presumably weren't killed during combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lawrence. I'm asking you, as an expert, because we have a problem here. People were placed in the grave throughout the whole battle front including those for which witnesses say were killed in fighting between the two sides, from a greater distance, and then they were buried together in various graves. So this is why I'm asking you how we can tell between those who were killed at close range and who were -- who were -- was killed from a greater distance. Thank you. I'm asking you for your expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If the question includes this fact, which it does, this proposed fact, then the witness should have the benefit of the reference for that fact to really be in a position to answer that sort of a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In particular the reference to graves from the -- in the battle front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you provide us with a reference, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I put a hypothetical question to the witness, and asked the witness, as an expert, to tell us, because we do have some cases. I'm going to be specific now. People who were killed in combat in the Zvornik area during the breakthrough of the Muslim column were collected and buried together with other casualties. Thank you. I didn't ask this for the purpose of just asking, but I asked in order to get expert indications, so that we can have an explanation by an expert. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just to be clear on the record that there is no evidence of those assertions, and if it's simply that this is all just hypothetical, then I think that should be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were referring to the Zvornik area. If you say that people were killed in combat in this area during the breakthrough of the Muslim column, then it's not a hypothetical question. Now, I'm a little bit confused. You should make it clear if you're putting a hypothetical question, or if you are referring to a specific grave or a number of graves, then you should give a reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I stated a fact that was stated here during testimony and footage about the breakthrough of the column from Zvornik towards -- actually near Nezuk, and people said, and you could see in the video footage, that there were about 2.000 killed and they were all buried in the same grave. And we have a problem here because all those who were found on the battlefield are now being counted as killed or executed and not those who died in fighting. So now I'm asking Mr. Lawrence for clarification about this. I am asking about testimony given by a particular witness. Ms. Hasan perhaps didn't hear the name but now I'm referring to it and I'm also stating it for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I didn't hear the name either. If you can give a name, everybody would be happy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said about Ms. Hasan actually, that she didn't mention her name when she was introducing herself, and I think we are talking about the ways that casualties were created. I am now seeking the clarification by this witness about possible ways in which this could have happened. This was something that was mentioned in the testimony of Mr. Janc. During his testimony I put certain questions to him because he put all the victims that were found into the same category. All the victims that were found in the same grave he would put in the same category. Thank you, Mr. President. It's not necessary even to have an answer to this question, if the Prosecution doesn't want to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not the right reaction. Mr. Lawrence, you have listened to this dispute. Perhaps you can help us with an answer that takes into account that this is a hypothetical statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can return to the start of the question, as I understand it, the issue that was being raised was it was important to tell the range of fire to try and distinguish between combatants and non-combatants. What I've indicated to you is I cannot tell you what the range of fire is. So in that context, I do not have information which would enable you to distinguish between combatants and non-combatants on the basis of range of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it possible that combatants who were killed in combat and those who were murdered end up in the same mass grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible. One wonders if that were the case, why one would conceal them if they were combatants, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. To follow up on the Presiding Judge's question, I have two questions. My first question: Can you, as a pathologist, determine whether people who are buried in the same mass grave come from two different sides [Realtime transcript read in error "sites"]? People who have been buried during combat or because they have been executed, do you think that people from the opposing side could be in the same mass grave? You mentioned the clothing, you mentioned the ligatures, and things like that. Are you able to determine that? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, let me make it clear that I did my work in the mortuary. I did attend some of the exhumation scenes. I went to Cancari 12, Cancari 3 and -- sorry, Liplje and Zeleni Jadar, but only on one day and not while -- I did not attend most of the time. Some of the issues in relation to whether the source of the bodies could have been from multiple sites should possibly be put to people who did their work at the scene, since they are probably in a better position than I am to comment on it, but it is possible that a grave could contain both combatants and people who had been executed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It wasn't two different sites but two different sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe you haven't quite understood what I was saying because you mention sides. When I talk about opponents, when I talk about the other side, I mean opponents in a war, different armed groups.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, sorry, I understand. The only comment I could make about working out whether somebody was Serbian, Bosnian Serbian or a Muslim would be the property that we found with the bodies. And all of the items which suggested a religious context suggested that all of the bodies that we could identify were Muslim. I guess it's possible there could have been other people. I also believe that subsequently most of these bodies have been identified as being Muslim people from Srebrenica but I'm not directly knowledgeable about that. It was work that was done after I worked for the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. My second question now. In your answer, you have already addressed my second question. It's on the transcript, page 36, line 2 to 4. You mention 193 cases. Out of these 183 cases, were you able to determine that these people belonged to the same armed group or whether some people came from the opposite side or the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, sorry, you mean 883 cases?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
