utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely, Dr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Look, I -- if you look at the end of each of the reports, I have indicated some additional identifying features. In only a very small number of cases in the graves did we find any material that might suggest that somebody was of Muslim faith. There was relatively little information. But the information that we did find indicated that the bodies that we saw were probably Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I thank you for your answer, Dr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, I just want a clarification and following up on Judge Mindua's question. At page 45, lines 6 to 8, you are reported -- recorded as saying: "And all of the items which suggested a religious context suggest that all of the bodies that we would could identify were Muslims." What sort of items would suggest that one is Muslim or not Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can just refer to my notes here, we have -- if I can refer you to the report on Hodzici Road number 3, at page 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P926.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As an example, page 20 there, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Perhaps it will assist if you can just give us the page number of your report and we will find the e-court number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the page number is 20 in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That would be e-court page 24.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you can look at Exhibit -- one of the exhibits, B11, we have verses from the Koran, which is just here. That sort of -- that was the material I was referring to that -- the only thing that we saw that would indicate the religion of the victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Lawrence, I didn't want to cause any kind of debate with my last question. I don't dispute that all the victims were Muslims. All I wanted to do was to talk about how distance is established because in the part where you discuss shrapnel, where I said in the other part, 5924 [as interpreted], page 22 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see that in e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you again referring to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P924.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the document we have on the screen at the moment. Sorry, that's a mistake. No, no. P924.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P924, page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the last paragraph, 22, where it says: "The distance from range of fire can sometimes be established by the presence or absence of muzzle abrasion, soot or abrasions caused by unburned gunpowder, gun powder stippling on the body or clothing. Due to the skeletonisation of the remains and the burial of the clothes, no assessment of range of fire was possible." All I was asking this is because it was not possible to establish the distance of fire, and we have cases that were described before. So all I wanted to ask you is to clarify for us, in cases where there is the presence of gunpowder, and you said you only had one such case, so I'm asking you about cases where there are no traces that you talk about in this text, how do you establish the distance of fire? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Lawrence
utterances.text: I have repeated this -- my answer several times. You can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise because of these polemics that was not my intention. My intention was to learn as much as possible from your testimony in order to be able to follow the issues and problems that occur during the trial, and I'm very grateful to you for providing answers about things that were unclear to me. I would like to thank you on behalf of the Defence. I would like to thank you for coming today. As far as I'm concerned, my part of the cross-examination is finished.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence would like to thank everybody, would like to thank everybody for their patience and would like to thank the interpreters and everyone else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you again for your kind words, Mr. Tolimir. Ms. Hasan, have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have no questions on re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lawrence, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your testimony. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here and now you are free to return to your normal activities. Thank you again that you could make it to come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Perhaps I can take some advantage perhaps so we can save some time. I see that on page 47, line 4, General Tolimir said that, and I quote, "I don't dispute that all the victims were Muslims." So can I offer General Tolimir an agreed fact based on this statement that he does not dispute that all the people in the mass graves that we have provided evidence for are Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was speaking here with this witness about those cases that he analysed and where he said on two occasions that this was 883 cases, and Mr. Mindua and myself put questions to him about this. I did not speak about anything else in the testimony today and I don't know why this question is being put when it did not include other things. I stressed twice and you also asked me whether I was thinking of 183 and I said that I meant 883. Mr. Mindua also asked and the witness also told him about 883 cases in question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That, of course, did not answer my question, but as he's representing himself, I believe that the Prosecution and the Court has a right to take him for his word when he says something like that, that he does not dispute that all the victims were Muslims, unless he wishes to withdraw it. He is now an officer of the Court and if he wishes to withdraw that statement, fair enough, as something he was just using in cross-examination. But I think we should be able to know whether or not he stands by that statement. And he knows that there were very few Serbs killed during this time-frame, and we have their hospital records in Zvornik, that they would not have, of course, put a Serb in a horrible mass grave like this. He knows that and that's why he made the statement. It's a fair statement. My question is: Will he stand by the statement and have the courage of his convictions or does he want to withdraw it? I think he needs to answer that question as an officer of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Everything is clear on the record. I just kindly ask Mr. McCloskey not minimise the Serbian victims in and around Srebrenica. I spoke about that several times during the trial. I would not now like to raise another dispute between me and Mr. McCloskey. But let us stick to the record and what we said for the record. I did not speak about the global issues that Mr. McCloskey is raising. If we are going down that path, then I can say I withdraw every statement that does not refer to Serbian victims in and around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we probably are gone about as far as we can go on that issue. I -- we'll take that answer on its face and our next scheduled witness is the continuation of Mr. Egbers and, of course, we have that Dutch interpreter issue. They are ready to go tomorrow morning but they are not here tonight, and I think this was a little earlier so I apologise but we don't have anyone ready to go right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what about the other two witnesses of this week, Mr. Blaszczyk and Ms. Gallagher?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know Mr. Thayer is currently with Mr. Blaszczyk going over the details of that testimony, trying to make sure we don't repeat some of what Ms. Gallagher testified to and to try to stick with the material that he is an expert with along the road, because it's that video that Ms. Gallagher showed you along the road that he is the expert at to show where exactly things are along the road. So I know that Mr. Thayer was working with him on that at the last break, and Ms. Gallagher is working on the -- her testimony to be ready for the Muslim identification book. I have not received an update with her on that but it would be a great surprise for her to come in right now. I had not prepared them to be ready to do that. Sometimes I do when I anticipate a break like this. I did not in this case, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the situation is quite unsatisfactory. If we would adjourn now for the day, we would lose one and a half hours of court time, or at least a little bit more than one hour. And I think it was indicated by the Prosecution to have one hour examination-in-chief, I think, 40 minutes were used, and the same occurred with the Defence. That may happen. But I, on behalf of the Chamber, would like to express my gratitude if both parties should take into account the possibility of an earlier end of an examination of a witness and there should always be one reserve witness available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Those generally match my instructions to my team, but we have taken into account the -- I'm not sure the General -- the amount of time the General has underestimated is very little. He gave us three hours here. So we took that at its word and figured, if anything, it may go over. I'm happy he didn't take that long for a pathologist after we had already seen a pathologist, but that's what we were basing that on. That's why I didn't have anyone prepared. To some degree we have to do -- we have to take them at their word but I don't fault General Tolimir in the slightest for being under time. But we will do our best, and I -- this is, of course, a very -- something I'm very familiar with and I know how important it is for the Court and I will work on the team on that point. We are -- just along this unfortunate topic. Mr. Thayer has been planning, as he must, for these subpoenaed witnesses because you must have dates on these subpoenas in order to give them -- have some value, and we are not -- as you know, this isn't a system where people jump. We are working on both those subpoenas. One is a little unclear whether the person is going to cooperate at all, but it's getting closer the more contact we have with the person related to the Skorpion situation. And the other person, it just now appears he's finally been served and it's an issue with visas and passports. And right now it's going to be very close, if at all, to get them in as planned. And that gives us a lot of trouble, and I will keep you informed up to the hour on that, because that becomes significant time problems for us. I am going to be myself hitting the road tomorrow to see witnesses personally, that live in Europe to try to convince them to come here. I have had several survivor witnesses that -- and frankly, DutchBat witnesses that have said, "I've been there three, four times," even some longer than that because of all the Srebrenica trials, "I can't do it anymore." This is something I'm hearing now for the first time in 12 years of doing this. And so I'm getting on the road to try to fill those gaps, but I hope I can come back with success for you. But we have not yet in this Office of the Prosecutor had to subpoena survivors of mass executions. I hope never to have to do that and -- but I've got significant witnesses now, Dutch witnesses, that are suffering from post-traumatic stress syndrome, victim witnesses that are worse. We are trying very hard but this is something I've not confronted with yet and it's something Mr. Thayer and I are working hard on. But we will keep you updated by the hour on this because, again, this is a very worsened thing for me, as I, as you know, do not want any wasted time or any down time in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I didn't want to criticise you. But we have heard your submission about your estimation of the length of the whole trial, I think two weeks ago, and we have to take into account to use the court time as best as possible. And therefore, I think the Chamber is aware of the problems you are facing, that I can understand everything you have just told us. And if, for instance, a victim, a survivor, is not willing to appear in court here, we should take into account the possibility of a videolink testimony and so on, but you're familiar with all these possibilities. But you still have the so-called gap-filling witnesses and this is a typical situation for calling a gap-filling witness. I see today you are not prepared to call one of them who are scheduled for this week. This is unfortunate but if it is not possible to call this witness or one of these two witnesses now, we can't do anything, but we would be very happy if you could try to avoid such a situation as we had today. The Chamber is always full of appreciation if the parties finish earlier their examination-in-chief or cross-examination, as it occurred today. This is always very helpful for the speed of the trial, but on the other hand, we should try to have always, in fact, a gap-filling witness, like it should be today. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I absolutely understand, Mr. President. We will do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything else to raise today? If there is nothing, we have to adjourn for the day and resume tomorrow in the morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of November, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.28 p.m.,
